items.title: Finding the Move Is Not Winning the Game: XiangqiBench for Closed-Loop Evaluation of LLM Agents
items.description:
arXiv:2610.02425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Static evaluations credit a language model for naming the right move, but an agent must carry a plan through to a verified outcome while an opponent responds. We introduce XiangqiBench, an executable benchmark that measures this difference in Chinese
items.summary: The paper introduces XiangqiBench, an executable benchmark for evaluating large language model agents in the game of Xiangqi by measuring their ability to execute plans through to a verified outcome rather than just naming correct moves. This matters because it provides a more realistic assessment of AI capabilities in strategic games where dynamic responses and long-term planning are crucial.
items.summary_detailed: Researchers have developed XiangqiBench, an executable benchmark for evaluating language model agents in the game of Xiangqi (Chinese chess), focusing on their ability to execute a complete strategy rather than just identifying correct moves. This tool aims to address the limitations of static evaluations by simulating dynamic gameplay scenarios where models must adapt and win against opponents. The broader impact could lead to more sophisticated training and testing methods for artificial intelligence agents in strategic games, enhancing their real-world applicability.
items.summary_bullets:
• XiangqiBench evaluates LLM agents' ability beyond just naming moves.
• It assesses the execution of plans and outcomes in response to opponents.
• The benchmark is designed for closed-loop evaluation in Chinese chess.

items.title: Counterexample Generation via Per-Theorem Symbolic Verifiers: When Imitation Hurts and Reinforcement Repairs
items.description:
arXiv:2610.02444v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models often solve a theorem forward yet fail to disprove a closely related false one: a falsification gap that supervised fine-tuning does not close and can actively worsen. We frame counterexample generation as constrained witness emi
items.summary: A study finds that large language models struggle to generate counterexamples for false theorems, even when trained on correct examples (the "falsification gap"). This issue persists despite supervised fine-tuning and requires new approaches like reinforcement learning to address.
items.summary_detailed: The study identifies a "falsification gap" where large language models struggle to generate counterexamples for false theorems, even when they can solve true ones correctly. Researchers propose using per-theorem symbolic verifiers to address this issue and find that supervised fine-tuning either does not close or sometimes exacerbates the gap. This work has implications for improving the robustness of AI systems in logical reasoning tasks.
items.summary_bullets:
• Large language models struggle with generating counterexamples for false theorems.
• Supervised fine-tuning fails to close the gap between solving true and false theorems.
• The gap can even be exacerbated by supervised methods.
• Counterexample generation is viewed through the lens of constrained witness emission.

schema_org.keywords: long-horizon tool-use, decision-making for complex tasks, value estimation for agents, reward-based decision making, comparative value estimation, large language models (llms), task state alteration, credit assignment problem
